Common questions from Lake County homeowners about remodeling projects

How much does a kitchen remodel cost in Lake County, IL?

Kitchen remodel costs in Lake County vary based on size, materials, and scope. A moderate kitchen renovation typically ranges from $25,000 to $75,000, while larger projects with custom cabinetry and high-end finishes can run higher. We provide free, detailed estimates so you know exactly what to expect before any work begins.

Do I need a permit for a remodeling project in Lake County?

Most structural work, electrical, plumbing, and additions require permits in Lake County municipalities like Grayslake, Libertyville, and Mundelein. Our team handles the permitting process for you, ensuring your project meets all local building codes and passes inspection the first time.

How long does a bathroom remodel take?

A typical bathroom remodel in our experience takes 2 to 4 weeks depending on the scope — whether it involves new tile work, plumbing relocation, or a full gut renovation. We keep you informed with clear timelines and regular communication throughout the project.

Do you offer free estimates for remodeling projects?

Yes! We offer free in-person estimates for homeowners in Lake County and the surrounding area, including Lindenhurst, Vernon Hills, Gurnee, Buffalo Grove, and beyond. We’ll walk through your project on-site so you get an accurate, no-pressure quote.

What areas in Lake County do you serve?

We serve homeowners within about a 20-mile radius of Lindenhurst, IL. That includes Grayslake, Libertyville, Mundelein, Vernon Hills, Gurnee, Barrington, Long Grove, Buffalo Grove, Lincolnshire, Lake Forest, Deerfield, Highland Park, Northbrook, Waukegan, and many more Lake County communities.

Can you help with room additions, garages, and deck construction?

Absolutely. In addition to interior remodeling, we build room additions, garages, decks, and handle exterior projects like painting and siding throughout Lake County. From planning and permits to the final walkthrough, we manage every detail of your project.

How is Rohrer for Construction different from other Lake County contractors?

We’ve been serving Lake County since 1989. Unlike companies that subcontract everything, the majority of our work is done in-house by our own experienced crew. That means better quality control, clearer communication, and a team that’s worked together for over 35 years. We’re licensed, insured, bonded, BBB accredited, and carry a 4.9-star review average.

One Contractor Managing the Bigger Picture

Hiring a general contractor is about more than finding someone to perform labor. It is about working with a company that can help organize the project, coordinate the moving parts, communicate clearly, and keep the work progressing in the right direction. At Rohrer for Construction, we help homeowners simplify that process by bringing project oversight under one roof.

Many remodeling and home improvement projects involve more complexity than they appear to at first. A kitchen may involve cabinetry, plumbing, electrical, flooring, trim, paint, and finish coordination. A bathroom remodel may involve demolition, tile work, waterproofing, fixture placement, ventilation, and final detailing. A basement, exterior, or garage project can introduce structural considerations, specialty materials, and site-related work that need to be handled in the right order.

As a general contractor in Lake County, IL, we help homeowners move those projects forward with a more organized process. Our work regularly includes kitchen remodeling, bathroom remodeling, basement finishing and remodeling, exterior remodeling, custom residential improvements, and broader home renovation work throughout Lake County.

Understanding Bathroom Remodel Pricing Factors in Lake County

Bathroom remodeling costs in Lake County, IL, are influenced by several key factors. Homeowners in Gurnee, Libertyville, and other areas often ask about budgeting, and understanding these elements is crucial for accurate planning. The primary drivers are the size of your bathroom, the extent of the renovation (e.g., partial refresh vs. complete gut and remodel), and your material selections.

Scope of Work

A simple cosmetic update, like new paint and vanity, will naturally cost less than a full renovation involving layout changes, plumbing relocation, or structural modifications. Moving walls or reconfiguring the shower and toilet typically incurs higher labor and material costs due to additional plumbing, electrical work, and permitting requirements.

Material Selections

From entry-level ceramic tiles to high-end natural stone or large-format porcelain, and from standard laminate countertops to quartz or granite, material choices significantly impact the budget. Fixtures such as Delta, Kohler, or Moen also range widely in price, affecting the overall investment. We guide you through options to balance aesthetics and budget.

Labor & Expertise

Our experienced crew and vetted subcontractors ensure professional, high-quality installation. While labor is a significant portion of the cost, investing in skilled craftsmen prevents costly errors and ensures a durable, code-compliant finish. This includes specialized work like Schluter waterproofing systems for showers.

Permits & Inspections

Many bathroom remodels in Lake County require permits, especially when altering plumbing, electrical, or structural components. These fees are a necessary part of the project to ensure safety and compliance with local building codes, adding a small but essential cost to the overall budget.

Customization & Features

Unique design elements like custom cabinetry, built-in storage, heated flooring, smart mirrors, steam showers, or specialized lighting schemes will increase the project cost. These features, however, often provide significant long-term value and enhance the spa-like feel of your new bathroom.

Accessibility Modifications

If your remodel includes aging-in-place features such as curbless showers, grab bar installations, or wider doorways, these specialized requirements will factor into the budget. These modifications improve safety and functionality, adding immense value for multi-generational living in your Lake County home.

Exploring Essential Materials and Options for Your Lake County Bathroom

The longevity and aesthetic of your bathroom remodel heavily depend on the materials you choose. In Lake County, where homes experience diverse weather patterns, selecting durable and moisture-resistant materials is paramount. We guide our clients through a curated selection of options, ensuring both beauty and resilience.

Flooring: Tile, LVT, and More

Porcelain and Ceramic Tile: These are classic choices for their water resistance, durability, and wide range of styles. Porcelain, being less porous, is excellent for high-moisture areas. Brands like Daltile and Marazzi offer extensive collections.

Luxury Vinyl Tile (LVT): A fantastic option for its waterproof properties, warmth underfoot, and ability to mimic wood or stone at a more accessible price point. Ideal for homeowners seeking both practicality and style.

Countertops: Quartz, Granite, and Solid Surface

Quartz: Engineered stone offering exceptional durability, stain resistance, and a non-porous surface, making it highly hygienic. Comes in a vast array of colors and patterns, including options that resemble natural stone.

Granite: A natural stone known for its unique patterns and strength. Requires periodic sealing but offers unparalleled elegance and heat resistance. Both are popular in upscale Lake County remodels.

Fixtures: Faucets, Showers, Toilets

Faucets & Shower Systems: We recommend trusted brands like Delta, Kohler, and Moen for their reliability, water efficiency, and design versatility. Options include thermostatic valves for precise temperature control and low-flow fixtures for water conservation.

Toilets: Comfort-height and dual-flush models are popular for both accessibility and water efficiency. Brands like Toto and American Standard lead the market in performance and design.

Waterproofing & Backer Board

Schluter Systems: For showers, we often utilize advanced waterproofing systems like Schluter-Kerdi. This integrated system ensures complete moisture management, preventing leaks and mold growth, which is critical in humid bathroom environments.

Cement Board: Provides a stable, water-resistant base for tiling walls and floors, superior to standard drywall in wet areas. Proper installation is key to preventing long-term issues.

Our team at Rohrer for Construction helps you navigate these choices, considering your budget, aesthetic preferences, and the specific demands of your Lake County home. Shower Enclosure Installation

A shower enclosure should fit the opening, contain water, and feel right to use every day. Rohrer for Construction coordinates shower enclosure installation as part of bathroom remodeling, from reviewing the shower area and selecting a door style to arranging installation and finishing details. We are a family-owned general contractor serving Lake County since 1989. Homeowners in Gurnee can request a free estimate to discuss a new enclosure or a larger bathroom update.

What shower enclosure installation includes

A well-planned enclosure is more than a glass panel or door. The opening must be measured, the shower walls and curb checked, and the enclosure style matched to how the bathroom is laid out. We review the existing conditions and discuss how the door will open, where water may reach, and how the finished enclosure will work with the rest of the room.

The project scope can include removing an existing enclosure, preparing the surrounding area, coordinating the glass and hardware, installing the selected enclosure, and completing related finish work. If the shower itself needs updating, we can plan the enclosure alongside tile, plumbing, or other bathroom remodeling work. Explore our bathroom remodeling services to see how a shower upgrade can fit into a broader project.

An enclosure replacement may be a focused improvement, while a remodel may be appropriate when the shower base, walls, or layout also need attention. We will clarify what is included in the project plan so you can make decisions based on the condition of your bathroom and the result you want.

Review of the shower opening, surrounding surfaces, and access
Planning for door movement, entry clearance, and hardware placement
Coordination of enclosure installation with related bathroom work
Finish details that help the enclosure work with the room
Choose an enclosure style and materials that suit the space

The right enclosure depends on the shower’s dimensions and the room around it. A sliding door can be useful where a hinged door would interfere with a vanity, toilet, or walkway. A hinged door needs enough clear floor area to swing open comfortably. Fixed glass panels can create an open feel, while a framed or semi-frameless design can provide a more defined edge around the glass.

Glass appearance, framing, hardware finish, and door configuration all affect the finished look. Clear glass keeps the tile visible; other glass treatments can offer more visual privacy. Frame and hardware choices can complement existing fixtures or be selected as part of a bathroom refresh. We help you compare practical options against the shape of the shower and the style of the room rather than choosing by appearance alone.

The surface behind the enclosure matters, too. Tile joints, curb shape, wall alignment, and the shower base influence how the enclosure can be fitted. In older Lake County homes—including ranches, split-levels, and colonials built from the 1950s through the 1990s—bathroom layouts and existing finishes can vary. We assess the actual opening before finalizing the plan, rather than assuming that a standard enclosure will fit.

Hardware finishes selected to coordinate with bathroom fixtures
When it is time to replace or add an enclosure

A shower door that no longer closes properly, glass that is damaged, or water escaping onto the bathroom floor are reasons to have the enclosure assessed. Changes to the bathroom—such as replacing the shower base, updating wall tile, or converting an older tub area—can also make a new enclosure part of the work. A door that blocks a walkway or conflicts with nearby fixtures may be a sign that a different configuration deserves consideration.

An enclosure alone may not address water that is getting behind tile or through a failed shower base. If the surrounding area shows persistent dampness, loose finishes, or damage, the underlying cause should be evaluated before new glass is installed. We can discuss whether the project is limited to the enclosure or should include related shower or bathroom work.

Winter freeze-thaw conditions in northern Illinois make sound exterior construction important, but the enclosure itself is an interior fixture. For bathrooms, the focus is on proper fit, sound surrounding surfaces, and keeping routine shower water within the intended wet area. Hard well or municipal water can leave mineral deposits on glass and hardware, so consider cleaning and upkeep when comparing glass and finish options.

A straightforward enclosure replacement may not involve the same approvals as a bathroom remodel that changes plumbing, electrical work, or the room’s structure. Shower Replacement and Remodeling

A worn, hard-to-clean shower can make an otherwise useful bathroom frustrating every day. Rohrer for Construction plans and builds shower replacements around your bathroom’s layout, your preferred materials, and the way your household uses the space. We are a family-owned local contractor serving Lake County and nearby McHenry County since 1989, and we handle permits when they are required. Request a free estimate to discuss your shower project.

Replace an aging shower with a better-fitting space

A shower replacement may be the right project when the base is cracked, grout or caulk keeps failing, water escapes the enclosure, or the surfaces are difficult to keep clean. You may also want to replace a tub-shower combination with a walk-in shower, improve access, or update a dated finish. If a leak or soft wall material suggests hidden moisture, the existing assembly should be assessed before new finishes go in.

Many local homes built from the 1950s through the 1990s have bathrooms sized around a standard tub or a compact shower. Ranches, split-levels, and colonials can each have different plumbing locations and framing conditions, so we look at the room before recommending a layout. Our bathroom remodeling service can address the shower as part of a broader bathroom update or as the main focus of the work.

The scope can include removing the old shower, preparing the walls and floor, installing a waterproofing system, fitting the selected surround and base, and adding fixtures and glass. The exact work depends on what is behind the existing finish and whether the plumbing or room layout needs to change.

Choose a shower layout and materials for daily use

A walk-in shower can use a curb or a low-threshold entry. A curbless design may make entry easier, but it requires careful coordination of floor height, drainage, and waterproofing; it is not suitable for every existing bathroom. We review the available space and conditions before settling on a plan. A hinged or sliding glass enclosure can help define the wet area, while a fixed panel may suit some open layouts.

Wall finishes can include tile or shower-rated panel systems. Tile offers choices in color, format, and pattern, but needs properly detailed waterproofing and grout maintenance. Panels reduce grout lines and create a more continuous surface. For the floor, the shower base and drain must work together; a tiled shower floor needs a suitable pitch and a surface selected with footing in mind. We can discuss practical tradeoffs as you choose finishes.

Think through storage and fixtures early. Recessed niches, corner shelves, a handheld shower, and a comfortable control location can make the space work better without changing the overall footprint. If you are comparing shower choices with the rest of a bathroom project, our bathroom remodeling overview is a useful place to start.

Plan for comfort, access, and local conditions

A shower remodel is worth considering when access has become difficult, a household’s needs have changed, or an old enclosure no longer fits your routine. A wider opening, a handheld shower, well-placed controls, and a bench may support easier use. Their fit depends on the room dimensions and the way water will be contained, so those details should be resolved before construction begins.

Freeze-thaw winters are part of life in this area, but the shower itself depends most on sound water management indoors: intact waterproofing, careful transitions, and a properly installed drain. Hard water from a well or municipal supply can also leave mineral deposits on glass and fixtures. Choosing finishes that suit your cleaning habits and using routine care can help keep the new shower presentable.

In Holiday Hills, in McHenry County, and Lakemoor, in Lake County, permit requirements can depend on the project scope and the authority responsible for the property. Changes to plumbing or electrical work may trigger review or inspections. We check applicable requirements and handle permits when needed rather than asking you to guess which forms apply. Choose a tub, surround, and finish that work together

Bathtubs come in different shapes, depths, and materials. Acrylic is a lighter-weight option with a smooth surface. Enameled steel and cast iron have different weight and feel characteristics. A heavier tub needs careful consideration of delivery access and floor support. We can compare options with the bathroom conditions and your preferences.

The wall area around the tub matters, too. Choices may include tile or a compatible panel surround. Tile allows flexibility in pattern and grout color. Panels offer a more continuous surface with fewer grout joints. We help coordinate the tub, wall finish, fixtures, and edge details so they work as one assembly.

The existing faucet location may be retained if the plumbing layout allows, or the project can include a different fixture arrangement as part of a wider remodel. In bathrooms with hard municipal or well water, mineral deposits can collect on fixtures and surfaces. Consider cleaning and upkeep when choosing finishes, and follow product care instructions.

If the tub is one part of a larger update, explore our bathroom remodeling service. We can discuss how the tub area will work with shower features and other bathroom finishes.

When replacement makes sense

A tub may need replacement when it is cracked, visibly worn, difficult to clean, or no longer suits the household. Persistent leaks, soft or damaged material around the tub, and signs of water behind the surround call for attention. The source and extent of moisture should be assessed before new finishes cover the area.

Replacement can also make sense during a bathroom refresh when the tub is the feature that no longer works. A different depth, shape, or configuration may better support your routine. If you are updating the room more broadly, it helps to coordinate the tub with flooring, wall finishes, ventilation, and storage.

Freeze-thaw winters are part of life in northern Illinois, although the tub itself is indoors. Local weather can matter when maintaining a home and protecting plumbing in colder areas. For a bathroom project, the key details are sound plumbing connections, suitable water protection, and well-finished transitions around the tub.

Tub-to-Shower Conversion in Lake County, IL

Replace an underused bathtub with a shower planned around your bathroom, daily routine, and home. Rohrer for Construction is a family-owned Lake County general contractor serving the area since 1989. Last reviewed/Updated: October 2026
Make the existing bathroom work harder

A tub-to-shower conversion can make a bathroom easier to use without changing the room’s overall footprint. Start by reviewing the tub, surrounding walls, plumbing locations, floor, and available clearance. Keeping fixtures near their current locations may limit plumbing work, while a different shower layout can add complexity.

Many Lake County homes built from the 1950s through the 1990s have ranch, split-level, or colonial layouts with bathrooms sized for a standard tub. A useful plan makes the most of the existing space rather than assuming a larger bathroom is necessary. We discuss layout, materials, and project scope through our bathroom remodeling services.

Measure the shower area and the route into the bathroom.
Review plumbing and visible finishes.
Choose a layout that suits the room and its users.
Choose shower details for comfort and upkeep

A conversion is a chance to decide what belongs in the shower, not just which tub comes out. Depending on the layout and products, options can include a low-threshold entry, built-in niche, handheld showerhead, bench or fold-down seat, and grab bars. Consider these choices together: a seat needs usable clearance, storage should be reachable, and grab bars need appropriate backing and placement.

Tile offers flexibility in color and pattern, while manufactured wall systems can reduce grout joints that need regular cleaning. Floor material, grout, hardware, and glass also affect daily maintenance. Lake County homes may have municipal water or private wells, and water mineral content can contribute to deposits on glass and fixtures. Check cleaning requirements for the products you are considering.

Northern Illinois freeze-thaw winters make reliable indoor moisture management important year-round. A properly planned shower assembly helps manage routine moisture; finish materials alone are not a substitute for a correctly installed waterproofing system.

Compare shower floors for slip resistance and cleaning needs.
Plan niches, seats, and grab bars before selecting wall finishes.
Choose glass and hardware with maintenance in mind.
Understand permits, plumbing, and the work area

Permit requirements depend on project scope and the jurisdiction responsible for the property. Bathroom work in Lake County may involve a village or city building department; Gurnee and Lindenhurst, for example, have local permit processes. Changes to plumbing, electrical, or structural components commonly trigger permit requirements. A finish update may be treated differently, so confirm the rules for your address and proposed work before construction starts.

Rohrer handles necessary permit applications as part of its planning process when the project requires them. We identify the proposed work and coordinate appropriate documentation and approvals before construction. For practical guidance, read our remodeling permit information and confirm local requirements with the authority having jurisdiction.

Ask which department reviews permits for your address.
Clarify whether plumbing, electrical, or structural changes are included.
Include permit and inspection requirements in the project plan.
Plan for the home you have

Older bathrooms can hold surprises behind the tub surround or beneath the floor. The substrate’s condition, previous repairs, and existing plumbing locations can affect the work required after demolition. A reliable scope distinguishes confirmed selections from conditions that cannot be assessed until materials are opened.

A shower can also change how a shared bathroom serves the household. In a ranch, split-level, or colonial, consider who uses the room and whether another bathtub remains available elsewhere. A walk-in shower may suit everyday access, while retaining a tub in a family bathroom may better meet household needs. We can discuss these tradeoffs as part of broader remodeling project planning.

Consider how the household uses this bathroom.
Decide which fixtures and accessories matter most.
Allow time to review concealed conditions found during demolition.
Set expectations for schedule and cost

There is no single timeline for every tub-to-shower conversion. The schedule depends on the work area, material selections and availability, permit or inspection requirements, plumbing changes, and conditions discovered during construction. A straightforward replacement with limited layout changes differs from work that relocates plumbing or requires repairs behind the existing tub. Your project plan should explain the sequence and identify decisions to make before construction begins.

Tub-to-shower conversion cost is shaped by the same scope choices. Keeping plumbing in place can reduce rework compared with moving fixtures, while tile, glass, built-in features, and concealed repairs affect the total. Rohrer’s site notes that moving or reconfiguring bathroom fixtures can require additional labor, plumbing, electrical work, and permitting. An estimate should be based on your room and selections, not a generic online figure. To outline the work, use the home remodeling scope builder.

Ask how permits and inspections affect the sequence.

04
Complete construction

Remove the existing tub, prepare the area, and complete planned plumbing, waterproofing, shower installation, and finish work.

05

Walk through the completed shower, review its features and care needs, and discuss any remaining project items.

Curbless Shower Installation

A curbless shower removes the raised threshold between the bathroom floor and shower, creating a cleaner transition and easier access. Rohrer for Construction plans and builds curbless showers as part of a bathroom remodel, coordinating the floor, drain, waterproofing, tile, glass and plumbing as one project. We are a family-owned local contractor serving Lake County since 1989. Request a free estimate to discuss your bathroom and the work needed to make a curbless design practical.

Written by Rohrer for Construction | Serving Lake County, IL since 1989 —
Last reviewed/Updated: October 2026
What a curbless shower includes

A curbless shower has no raised curb to step over. Its floor is set up to direct water toward a drain while keeping the bathroom floor outside the shower protected. The finished result depends on more than tile: the shower base, waterproofing, drain location, floor height and enclosure must work together.

The scope can include removing an existing tub or shower, adjusting plumbing, preparing or modifying the floor, installing a waterproofing system, setting tile, fitting glass and installing new fixtures. If the project is part of a broader bathroom remodeling project, we can also plan the shower alongside the vanity, lighting and other room finishes.

Before design decisions are final, we assess the existing floor and drain route. Some bathrooms can accommodate a recessed shower area; others need a different floor or drain plan. In older homes, the available framing depth and existing plumbing can affect what is feasible. A site review helps identify those constraints before materials are selected.

A carefully sloped shower floor that directs water to the drain
A waterproofed shower assembly, including vulnerable transitions
Drain, fixture and glass choices coordinated with the layout
Tile installation and finishing around the shower opening
Choose materials and details for daily use

Tile selection affects appearance, cleaning and footing. Porcelain is a common choice for shower floors and walls because it is available in many formats and finishes. Smaller mosaic pieces can follow a sloped floor more readily and provide more grout lines underfoot; larger wall tile can create a simpler visual pattern. Natural stone is another option, but it may call for more attention to sealing and routine care.

A point drain is typically placed within the shower floor, while a linear drain can sit along an edge or wall when the layout supports it. The drain choice influences how the floor is shaped and where cuts in the tile fall. Grout color, trim, niche placement and shower controls should be considered at the same time so the finished surfaces look intentional and are practical to maintain.

Glass can keep the bathroom feeling open, while a fixed panel or door configuration helps contain spray. Handheld showerheads and well-positioned controls can make the space more convenient. Grab bars can be included in the design, with blocking planned behind the finished wall where needed. A curbless shower alone does not guarantee accessibility; clearances, controls, support and the rest of the bathroom layout matter too.

Porcelain, ceramic or natural-stone tile, selected for the intended use
Mosaic or larger-format tile suited to the floor layout
Point or linear drain, based on the room and slope plan
Glass enclosure, handheld showerhead, niche and optional support bars

When a curbless shower may be a good fit

Homeowners often consider a curbless shower when replacing a tub, updating an aging bathroom or making entry easier for someone who finds a high step difficult. It can also suit a bathroom where a low-profile, open shower is a design priority. Think about who uses the room, how much splash containment you need, and whether the shower can fit without compromising other bathroom functions.

Many Lake County homes built from the 1950s through the 1990s—including ranches, split-levels and colonials—have bathroom layouts and floor assemblies that were not designed around a curbless shower. The existing plumbing and framing may limit how the shower floor can be lowered. A successful plan accounts for those conditions rather than assuming the new shower can simply replace the old base.

Freeze-thaw winters make a dry, usable bathroom especially important, but they do not change the need for sound shower detailing. Water must be directed into the drain and kept within the waterproofed area. If your home has hard water, mineral deposits may show on glass and fixtures, so choose finishes with cleaning and upkeep in mind. We can review these considerations during an estimate visit.

Replacing a tub or raised shower threshold
Improving access for changing mobility needs
Updating an older bathroom while keeping the room’s layout workable

A shower remodel that changes plumbing, electrical work or other regulated components may require a permit. Requirements depend on the property’s jurisdiction and project scope; a village may have its own application and inspection process. We review the applicable requirements, prepare and submit permit applications when needed, and coordinate required inspections as part of the project.

Rohrer has served Lake County since 1989 and handles permits for remodeling work. If your home is in Grayslake, the local building department’s process is one part of planning the schedule. We confirm the requirements for the actual project rather than relying on a general assumption. Learn more about our permit process or check the county’s building permit information. You can also learn about Rohrer for Construction and our local experience.

Permit applications are only one part of the preparation. The shower design, material selections and construction plan need to be clear enough to guide the work. Our team discusses the scope with you before construction begins and keeps the project tied to the approved plan.

Plan plumbing, floor preparation, waterproofing and finish details together
Coordinate required applications and inspections
Curbless Shower Installation Timeline

A curbless shower project typically moves from planning and material selection through construction and final checks. The ranges below are planning estimates, not guarantees; the actual timeline depends on the design, project scope and any applicable permit process.

Design and project planning
1–2 weeks

Discuss the shower layout, materials and project scope. The team can help review options such as tile and Schluter waterproofing systems.

Plans and permit coordination
1–3 weeks

Once the design is finalized, plans and material specifications are developed. If permits apply to the work, the process includes preparing applications and coordinating with the local building department before construction begins.

Shower construction
1–3 weeks

The existing shower area is prepared and the new curbless shower is built. Changes to plumbing or other parts of the bathroom can affect the work involved and the timeline.

Finishing and final checks
3–7 days

Complete the selected finishes and review the finished work. If the project requires inspections, their timing may affect completion.

Our curbless shower installation process

We start by understanding the bathroom as it exists, then plan the shower around the home, the way you use the space and the work required to build it.

We look at the current shower or tub, bathroom dimensions, access, plumbing and visible floor conditions. You can share priorities such as easier entry, a particular tile style, storage or new fixtures.

We determine whether the floor can support a curbless design and discuss drain placement, floor slope, enclosure, tile and fixture options. If the existing conditions call for a different approach, we explain the practical choices.

03

We confirm the project details and selections, prepare the construction plan and handle applicable permit applications. Local review and inspections are coordinated according to the requirements for the property and work.

04
4. Build and finish the shower

The team completes demolition and necessary preparation, then installs the planned shower components, waterproofing, tile, fixtures and glass. We coordinate the work so the drain, floor and enclosure fit the finished design.

05
5. Review the completed work

We review the finished project with you, explain care considerations for the selected materials and address any remaining project items.

A good design balances access, water control and the look you want.

Floor and drain

The shower floor needs a deliberate slope to the drain. Floor height and existing framing help determine the workable design.

Waterproofing

A curbless opening needs careful detailing at the shower floor, walls and transitions to keep water within the intended area.

Tile and upkeep

Choose floor tile suited to the slope and intended use. Consider grout, stone care and hard-water deposits when comparing finishes.

Access and enclosure

Plan glass, controls, storage and optional grab bars around the people using the bathroom and the space available.

Kitchen Remodeling That Improves Everyday Living, Function, and Home Value

A kitchen should support the way your household actually lives. It should feel practical, organized, easy to use, and visually connected to the rest of the home. At Rohrer for Construction, we help homeowners throughout Lake County transform outdated kitchens into modern, functional spaces built around better layouts, smarter storage, quality finishes, and long-term daily usability.

Kitchen Remodel Contractor Services for Lake County Homes

The kitchen is one of the most used spaces in the home. It is where meals are prepared, daily routines overlap, conversations happen, and family life tends to gather. When the layout is awkward, storage is limited, finishes are worn, or the room simply feels outdated, the entire home can feel less functional.

A well-planned kitchen remodel gives homeowners the chance to improve more than just the look of the space. It can make cooking easier, improve traffic flow, create more usable work surfaces, increase storage, and better connect the kitchen to the rest of the home. The goal is not just a prettier room. The goal is a room that works better every day.

Many kitchen remodeling clients also end up exploring bathroom remodeling, basement renovation, or broader general contractor services as part of improving the home as a whole.

What a Kitchen Remodel Can Improve
Better layout and easier movement through the room
Improved cabinet storage and pantry organization
More efficient countertop and prep space
Updated flooring, backsplash, and finish selections
Improved lighting and appliance placement
Cleaner visual flow with the rest of the home
More functional islands and seating areas
Stronger resale appeal and long-term value
Types of Kitchen Remodeling Projects We Handle
Full Kitchen Renovations

A full kitchen renovation is ideal when the room needs a major refresh in layout, finishes, cabinets, countertops, lighting, and overall function. These projects give homeowners the chance to rethink the space from the ground up.

Kitchen Layout Improvements

Some kitchens look acceptable on the surface but still function poorly. Layout-focused remodeling can improve work flow, increase usable prep space, and create a better relationship between cooking, storage, and seating areas.

Small Kitchen Remodeling

Smaller kitchens often require the smartest planning. Better cabinet design, efficient layouts, improved lighting, and strategic storage can make compact kitchens feel more capable without needing extra square footage.

Open Concept Kitchen Updates

When homeowners want the kitchen to feel more open and connected to nearby living or dining space, remodeling can help create a cleaner and more inviting flow throughout the main level of the home.

Popular Kitchen Remodeling Upgrades
Cabinetry, Storage, and Organization

Storage is one of the biggest reasons homeowners remodel a kitchen. Cabinet layout, pantry solutions, drawer systems, and island storage all affect how well the room works. Better cabinetry planning can reduce clutter, improve access, and make the room more enjoyable to use every day.

A kitchen should not force you to work around poor storage decisions. It should support the way you cook, clean, gather, and live.

Countertops, Surfaces, and Finishes

Countertops, flooring, backsplashes, and finish selections shape both the appearance and practicality of the kitchen. The right materials should feel cohesive with the home while also standing up to real daily wear.

A successful remodel balances style with durability. Homeowners should not have to choose between a kitchen that looks good and a kitchen that performs well.

How Kitchen Remodeling Impacts Cost

Kitchen remodeling costs vary based on the size of the room, the complexity of the project, the material selections, and whether the remodel includes layout changes, electrical work, plumbing adjustments, or appliance repositioning. Keeping the general footprint similar is usually more straightforward than redesigning the entire room.

The more moving parts a project has, the more important planning becomes. That is why scope, material choices, and realistic budgeting should be clarified early.

If you are in the planning stage, it may help to review our Kitchen Remodeling Cost Estimator, browse the Advice Center, or review Remodel Financing Options for Lake County homeowners.

Some kitchen projects may also require permit coordination depending on the work involved, and our Building Permits Made Easy resources can help explain what to expect.

Our Kitchen Remodeling Process
01
Consultation

We start by learning about your kitchen, your goals, your layout frustrations, and the kind of finished result you want from the remodel.

02
Planning

Layout direction, cabinet planning, finish selections, budgeting, and any permit-related considerations are organized before construction begins.

03
Construction

Once the scope and selections are set, the project moves into execution with a focus on craftsmanship, detail, and communication.

04
Final Walkthrough

We review the completed kitchen together and make sure the finished space aligns with the original plan and expectations.

Designed for Everyday Life, Not Just Showrooms
A Better Kitchen Should Feel Better to Use

A kitchen can have beautiful finishes and still be frustrating if the layout, storage, lighting, and appliance placement are not planned well. The best kitchen remodels improve both form and function so the room feels more useful every single day.

That is why kitchen remodeling should consider more than cabinets and countertops. Traffic flow, work surfaces, seating, organization, and how the room connects to nearby living space all matter.

If you are still comparing options, you can browse Home Remodeling FAQs, explore Our Work, or read Our Reviews to get a better feel for the process.

Kitchen Storage & Pantry Remodeling

Storage planned around your kitchen

Kitchen storage remodeling can be a focused update or part of a broader kitchen renovation. We look at how the room is used, what needs a home and where storage is hard to reach. The goal is to make everyday items easier to put away and find without adding clutter to counters.

Options may include replacing cabinets, adjusting cabinet layouts, adding drawer storage, fitting pull-out shelves, creating a pantry cabinet or improving an existing pantry with new shelving. For a larger change, storage planning can be included in a complete kitchen remodeling project.

The right scope depends on the condition of the existing cabinets, available wall space, appliance locations and whether plumbing or electrical work is part of the plan. We discuss those details before construction so you can compare practical options rather than choose storage pieces in isolation.

Cabinet and drawer layouts suited to daily cooking and cleanup
Pantry shelving or cabinet storage sized to the available space
Finish and hardware selections that coordinate with the rest of the kitchen
Cabinets, pantry options and materials

A pantry can be a dedicated closet, a bank of tall cabinets or a combination of shelves and drawers. In a smaller kitchen, tall cabinetry can use vertical space while keeping frequently used items accessible. In a larger room, a walk-in pantry or reworked cabinet arrangement may be worth considering if the layout allows it.

Cabinet choices range from stock sizes to semi-custom and custom configurations. Interior features can include adjustable shelves, deep drawers, tray dividers and pull-out storage. Door styles, finishes, knobs and pulls help the new storage fit the kitchen’s overall look. For shelves, we can discuss durable finished surfaces and spacing based on the items you plan to store.

Countertops, backsplash, flooring and lighting may also be part of a wider remodel. If you are considering a full refresh, our project portfolio offers examples of completed work. Final material selections should suit your maintenance preferences and the conditions in the room.

Cabinet boxes and fronts selected for the project scope
Adjustable pantry shelves and drawer inserts
Hardware and finishes coordinated with existing or new surfaces
When better kitchen storage makes sense

Storage is worth addressing when cabinets are difficult to reach, shelves are poorly sized, pantry contents get lost or counters have become the default place for appliances and supplies. A remodel can also be a good time to correct storage that no longer suits a household’s routines or to plan for changing needs.

Many homes in the area were built from the 1950s through the 1990s, including ranches, split-levels and colonials. Their kitchen layouts and cabinet sizes can reflect the priorities of a different era. When we assess an existing kitchen, we consider its dimensions and conditions rather than assume modern cabinet sizes or a new layout will fit without adjustments.

Some homeowners want a targeted pantry renovation; others are already planning new cabinets, counters or a broader kitchen remodel. If the work changes walls, plumbing or electrical systems, permit needs may depend on the scope and the local jurisdiction. We coordinate permits for our projects and can help explain the steps; our permit resources outline what homeowners can expect.

Cabinets with awkward access or wasted interior space

Making those decisions together helps keep finish choices and construction sequencing aligned. Cabinet types, materials, and useful options

Cabinets are available in stock, semi-custom, and custom configurations. Stock cabinets use standard sizes and a defined selection of finishes. Semi-custom lines offer more choice in dimensions, door styles, and interior features. Custom cabinets allow greater flexibility when a kitchen has unusual dimensions or a specific design requirement. The right fit depends on your room, storage priorities, finish preferences, and project scope—not simply on choosing the most elaborate option.

Material choices can include solid wood, plywood, and engineered products such as medium-density fiberboard. Each has different characteristics, and construction details matter alongside the material name. Door styles range from simple slab fronts to framed and raised-panel designs. You can also consider painted or stained finishes, soft-close hinges and slides, pull-out shelves, drawer organizers, and pantry storage. We help you compare practical options and coordinate cabinet selections with counters, flooring, and backsplash finishes.

Planning for older Lake County kitchens

Many local homes built from the 1950s through the 1990s—including ranches, split-levels, and colonials—have kitchens shaped by the original floor plan. A replacement cabinet plan may need to account for soffits, uneven walls, older flooring, or appliance locations that limit standard cabinet sizes. Measuring the room carefully and checking what is behind the existing finishes helps set a realistic scope before installation begins.

Freeze-thaw winters are part of life in this region, but indoor cabinet performance is most directly affected by normal household conditions such as moisture, heat, and ventilation. We consider how cabinets meet the walls and floor, how doors and drawers will function in tight spaces, and whether the layout gives you practical access to dishes, cookware, and supplies. Homeowners in Round Lake Heights and Hainesville can request a free estimate to review their kitchen’s specific constraints and goals.

When replacement makes sense

Cabinet replacement may be worth considering when boxes are damaged, shelving no longer meets your needs, doors and drawers are difficult to use, or the current layout wastes available space. It can also be a sensible part of a kitchen update when the cabinets’ condition or style conflicts with other planned work. If the cabinet boxes are sound and the layout works, ask us whether a more limited update could meet your priorities; replacement is not automatically the right answer for every kitchen.

A cabinet project is also a chance to correct practical frustrations: too little drawer storage, hard-to-reach corner shelves, a crowded cooking area, or a pantry that does not hold everyday items well. Before choosing products, make a short list of what currently works and what does not. In Round Lake Park, as elsewhere in the service area, we can use that list to guide choices and explain how cabinet installation fits a larger renovation. Permits and project coordination

Permit needs depend on the work involved and the rules of the authority serving your property. A cabinet-only change may differ from a project that alters plumbing, electrical systems, walls, or the kitchen footprint. We review the scope and handle permit coordination when permits are required, so the right steps are part of planning rather than an afterthought. Local requirements can vary; the responsible village or county office determines applicable approvals.

Our permit resources explain what homeowners can expect, and you can consult the county’s building permit information as a starting point. If you are still defining the work, the scope builder can help organize project ideas before we discuss them.
